target.title: RFC: Readiness Conditions and Standard Hosting Profiles
target.body:
## Decision requested

Should OpenClaw adopt one canonical readiness-condition model and a small set of standard, release-testable hosting profiles?

The proposed v1:

1. normalizes existing Gateway readiness observations into structured required and advisory conditions;
2. defines `local`, `container`, `reverse-proxy`, and `node-mode` profiles;
3. lets activated plugins contribute bounded observational conditions that are advisory by default;
4. lets operator profiles extend, but never weaken, a standard profile; and
5. projects one authoritative result through `/ready`, `/readyz`, health, status, and the optional `openclaw ready` CLI.

This does **not** add a policy engine, OCC dependency, Lobster abstraction, new control plane, or second configuration system.

## Why this is needed

OpenClaw can run in a container today, but a live process does not prove that the selected runtime posture can serve work.

Examples include:

- a container starts while its effective Gateway listener remains loopback-only;
- the Gateway responds while its workspace cannot be written;
- a node controller starts before an approved controllable target is connected;
- a required plugin-owned dependency is unavailable; and
- a reverse proxy is selected without a valid trusted-forwarder configuration.

Hosts currently close these gaps with private scripts and downstream-specific probes. OpenClaw also has useful Gateway readiness observations today, but they are evaluated by a fixed-purpose path rather than an enumerable condition contract that profiles and plugins can extend.

## Proposed contract

Every condition has a stable shape:

```text
type + status + requirement + reason + message
```

- `required` conditions with status `False` or `Unknown` make readiness fail.
- `advisory` conditions remain visible without changing readiness success.
- Existing startup, drain, selected-channel, suppressed-channel, and event-loop observations become canonical core conditions.
- Existing `failing`, `suppressed`, and `eventLoop` fields remain compatibility projections during migration.
- Profiles and plugins cannot weaken universal Gateway lifecycle conditions.
- `/healthz` remains shallow liveness.

A readiness provider is activation-scoped plugin code registered through `OpenClawPluginApi`. Providers are read-only, idempotent, cancellation-aware, bounded by code-owned deadlines, and advisory unless an operator explicitly promotes the condition to required. Operators and OCC may select profiles and provider IDs; they cannot inject executable callbacks.

## Standard profiles

| Profile | Runtime posture | Additional required evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | Default local or foreground Gateway | Valid effective config, usable workspace, and Gateway lifecycle |
| `container` | Gateway directly reachable through a container listener | Effective listener is non-loopback |
| `reverse-proxy` | Gateway behind a trusted identity proxy | Trusted-proxy identity header and trusted source |
| `node-mode` | Gateway controlling execution targets | Pairing, connected target, command approval, and control channel |

A profile describes runtime posture, not packaging. Docker behind an identity proxy selects `reverse-proxy`; directly reachable Docker selects `container`. Existing installations default to `local`.

Standard profiles are valuable as a support contract: OpenClaw can release-test a known subset of valid deployments, users can report the selected profile with diagnostics, and hosts can use the same readiness result in Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, OCC, or another scheduler.

## Host-visible behavior

A container profile with a loopback-only listener returns:

```http
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
```

```json
{
  "profile": "container",
  "ready": false,
  "conditions": [
    {
      "type": "ContainerStateReady",
      "status": "False",
      "requirement": "required",
      "reason": "ContainerGatewayLoopback"
    }
  ],
  "failures": ["ContainerGatewayLoopback"]
}
```

After the effective listener becomes reachable, the same endpoint returns `200`. The host does not switch APIs or interpret a second health model.

A failed plugin condition remains advisory and returns `200` unless an operator profile explicitly makes that provider required. Promotion changes the same result to `503`; recovery returns it to `200` without restarting OpenClaw.

## Scope and ownership

OpenClaw owns the condition schema, core evaluators, profile definitions, provider lifecycle, canonical result, and release conformance for standard profiles.

Hosts own profile selection, probe timing, retries, placement, tenant routing, policy rollout, telemetry sinks, and operational response.

OCC may select profiles as desired state, but readiness remains in the runtime/data plane. AgentHarness traffic and events are outside this contract. Configuration authority and state continuity remain separate contracts; a runtime can be ready but not safely checkpointed, or not ready while its durable state is complete.

## Implementation and proof

The consolidated draft implementation is [openclaw/openclaw#104018](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104018).

Smaller review slices remain available:

| Slice | Draft PR |
| --- | --- |
| Core conditions and local profile | [PR 17](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/17) |
| Standard profile selection | [PR 18](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/18) |
| Node-mode readiness | [PR 19](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/19) |
| Workspace writability | [PR 22](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/22) |
| Readiness providers and operator profiles | [PR 23](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/23) |
| Canonical readiness CLI | [PR 27](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/27) |

At implementation head `153d413b25cefa8b44978ff16bece0604863d9af`:

- 196 focused readiness, Gateway, status, package-acceptance, and Docker-planning assertions passed.
- The complete package-installed Docker lane passed on sanitized AWS Crabbox.
- Validated scenarios include local readiness; container success and loopback failure; reverse-proxy success and missing-auth failure; node-mode unpaired and approved transitions; and workspace-full failure and recovery.
- Provider, workspace, and node checks have explicit deadlines plus an independent outer watchdog so `/ready` and `/readyz` fail closed rather than hang.

## Staged follow-ups

These are intentionally separable from accepting the core v1 contract:

- [PR 42](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/42) adds runtime activation identity so a readiness result can identify the logical runtime and process/container incarnation it describes.
- [PR 21](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/21) demonstrates making packaged profile conformance release-blocking. That governance change should follow contract acceptance and repeatable packaged proof.
- Stable transition events and Doctor/lint recommendations can follow without becoming dependencies of core readiness.
- Additional owners may publish conditions through the same contract; readiness does not absorb their configuration, credentials, traffic, or state semantics.

## Maintainer questions

1. Is the required/advisory condition model the right canonical replacement for the fixed-purpose readiness evaluator?
2. Should OpenClaw own these four standard profiles as release-tested support contracts?
3. Should plugin providers and derived operator profiles be included in v1, or staged after core condition normalization and standard profiles?

The full schema, compatibility rules, failure behavior, security considerations, and implementation roadmap are in the RFC.
